Super Coalition Number in Graphs

Saeid Alikhani Note: Corresponding author    Nima Ghanbari
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We introduce and investigate the structural properties of super coalition partitions in graphs, a novel direction that bridges cooperative resource deployment with rigid domination criteria. Based on the foundational concept of super domination, a super coalition partition is defined as a vertex set partitioning Υ={A1,A2,…,Ak}\Upsilon=\{A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{k}\} such that no single class AiA_{i} constitutes a valid super dominating set, yet every class can be paired with at least one distinct partner class AjA_{j} to form a union Ai∪AjA_{i}\cup A_{j} that achieves full super domination over the graph. The super coalition number, denoted by Cs​(G)C_{s}(G), represents the maximum possible cardinality of such a partition. In this paper, we establish general operational bounds for Cs​(G)C_{s}(G) using the underlying order and the super domination number γs​p​(G)\gamma_{sp}(G), demonstrate its relation to the super domatic number ds​p​(G)d_{sp}(G), analyze its computational complexity proving its NP-complete nature under general conditions, and provide exact determinations for key standard graph architectures including paths, cycles, complete graphs, stars, wheels, and friendship configurations. We conclude by proving that the super coalition number can grow arbitrarily large.

Keywords: Super domination, Coalition partition, Super coalition number.

1 Introduction

In modern network analysis, graph theory serves as a fundamental mathematical language for modeling interconnected systems, failure propagation, security infrastructure, and distributed control systems. Within this realm, domination theory forms a major core branch of optimization study. Classical domination concerns the identification of a minimum subset of nodes whose immediate neighborhoods encompass all remaining nodes in the graph. This formulation efficiently models resource location problems where a central node can readily service or monitor its neighbors. However, standard domination models often fall short when dealing with highly secured networks, decentralized environments, or cooperative defense settings where components lack individual strength but must operate collectively to protect or access information.

To address scenarios where solitary tracking components or regional subsets are intrinsically insufficient to dominate an entire network topology, Haynes et al. [12] pioneered the concept of coalition domination in 2020. A coalition within a graph consists of two or more disjoint vertex sets that are individually incapable of dominating the graph, but whose collective union forms a valid dominating configuration. This mathematical framework represents a shift toward cooperative game-theoretic properties within discrete combinatorial optimization.

Following this seminal work, coalition parameters have been generalized and examined across multiple structural domains. Alikhani et al. [2] explored total coalitions in graphs, where the combined sets must form a total dominating set, ensuring that every vertex in the graph possesses a neighbor within the dominating coalition. In 2025, Alikhani, Bakhshesh, Golmohammadi, and Klavžar [3] introduced independent coalitions, imposing the constraint that the partnering sets or the resulting coalition must maintain an independent internal structure, which introduces profound challenges regarding independent partitioning. Concurrently, the study of connected coalitions [4] demanded that the induced subgraph of the union must be connected, reflecting practical demands in communication systems where tracking sensors must remain continually linked to pass information securely.

In parallel with the development of these cooperative frameworks, researchers have extensively investigated specialized, high-security variants of classical domination. Among these, the notion of super domination, originally conceptualized by Lemańska et al. [14], represents a powerful constraint model. In a standard dominating set SS, a vertex u∉Su\notin S must simply have at least one neighbor in SS. In stark contrast, a super dominating set requires that for every vertex u∈S¯=V∖Su\in\overline{S}=V\setminus S, there must exist an internal vertex v∈Sv\in S that super dominates uu, meaning that the entire open neighborhood of vv outside of SS contains precisely and uniquely the single vertex uu. This restriction creates a strong structural isolation for the external vertices: each external node is strictly locked to a specific internal anchor vertex which has no other external connections.

Super domination has proved to be highly receptive to structural analysis but remarkably rigid. Extensive literature has accumulated surrounding its properties. Alfarisi et al. [1] explored the behavior of super domination in unicyclic networks, while Akbari et al. [6] addressed specialized end super dominating parameters. To understand how graphs combine under this strict criterion, Dettlaff et al. [8] derived expressions for the super domination number across lexicographic product graph configurations.

Furthermore, the fundamental structural aspects, enumeration methodologies, and behaviors across various algebraic graph architectures were detailed comprehensively by Ghanbari, Jäger, and Lehtilä [11] in 2024. Computational complexity investigations conducted by Bǔjtas, Ghanbari, and Klavžar [7] established that determining the super domination number remains an NP-hard problem even when restricted to specialized graph subfamilies, reflecting the intricate non-local interactions forced by the super domination condition. Additional foundational results regarding bounds, exact sequences, and functional relationships are detailed in the literature [9, 10, 13, 15].

Despite the extensive research devoted to standard coalition frameworks and the distinct structural investigations into super domination parameters, cooperative behavior under the rigid neighborhood isolation of super domination has remained unexplored. Motivated by this clear research gap, this paper formally introduces the concept of super coalition partitions in graphs. This parameter integrates the cooperative distribution properties of coalitions with the highly restrictive neighborhood constraints of super domination.

The text is organized as follows: Section 2 outlines essential notations, reviews key known theorems, and establishes the basic properties of super coalitions. Section 3 focuses on general upper and lower bounds on the super coalition number, explicitly relating it to the underlying order, the super domination number, and the super domatic number. Section 4 provides a formal verification of the computational complexity, demonstrating that the underlying decision problem is NP-complete. Section 5 presents exact structural computations of the parameter for several core graph families, including paths, cycles, complete setups, star graphs, wheels, and friendship graphs. In Section 6 we prove that the super coalition number can be arbitrarily large. We conclude the paper by brief conclusions and an open problem outline in Section 7.

2 Preliminaries

Throughout this work, we consider only finite, simple, and undirected graphs G=(V⁡(G),E⁡(G))G=(V(G),E(G)). For any vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), its open neighborhood is denoted by N⁡(v)={w∈V⁡(G):v​w∈E⁡(G)}N(v)=\{w\in V(G):vw\in E(G)\}, and its closed neighborhood is N⁡[v]=N⁡(v)∪{v}N[v]=N(v)\cup\{v\}. The degree of a vertex vv is given by deg⁡(v)=|N⁡(v)|\deg(v)=|N(v)|. For a subset S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G), the complement set is denoted by S¯=V⁡(G)∖S\overline{S}=V(G)\setminus S.

A set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is a dominating set if every vertex in S¯\overline{S} is adjacent to at least one vertex in SS. The domination number γ⁡(G)\gamma(G) is the minimum cardinality of a dominating set in GG.

A dominating set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is a super dominating set if for every vertex u∈S¯u\in\overline{S}, there exists a vertex v∈Sv\in S such that N⁡(v)∩S¯=N⁡(v)∖S={u}N(v)\cap\overline{S}=N(v)\setminus S=\{u\}. Under these conditions, vv is said to super dominate uu. The super domination number of GG, denoted by γs​p​(G)\gamma_{sp}(G), is the cardinality of a minimum super dominating set of GG [14].

We now introduce the foundational terms for our cooperative framework.

Definition 2.1

Let GG be a graph. Two disjoint subsets A1,A2⊆V⁡(G)A_{1},A_{2}\subseteq V(G) form a super coalition in GG if:

  • (i)

    neither A1A_{1} nor A2A_{2} is a super dominating set of GG, and

  • (ii)

    the union A1∪A2A_{1}\cup A_{2} forms a valid super dominating set of GG.

Definition 2.2

A super coalition partition of a graph GG is a partition

Υ={A1,A2,…,Ak}\Upsilon=\{A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{k}\}

of the vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) such that:

  • (i)

    no part Ai∈ΥA_{i}\in\Upsilon is a super dominating set of GG, and

  • (ii)

    for every part Ai∈ΥA_{i}\in\Upsilon, there exists at least one distinct part Aj∈ΥA_{j}\in\Upsilon (j≠ij\neq i) such that Ai∪AjA_{i}\cup A_{j} forms a super dominating set of GG.

The class AjA_{j} described above is termed a super coalition partner of AiA_{i}.

Definition 2.3

The super coalition number of a graph GG, denoted by Cs​(G)C_{s}(G), is the maximum cardinality of a super coalition partition of GG. If a graph GG does not admit any super coalition partition, we state that Cs​(G)=0C_{s}(G)=0.

We now establish a basic bounding lemma regarding the size of the individual parts within any valid partition.

Lemma 2.4

Let GG be a graph that admits a super coalition partition Υ={A1,A2,…,Ak}\Upsilon=\{A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{k}\}. Then k≥2k\geq 2, and for every i∈{1,2,…,k}i\in\{1,2,\ldots,k\}, the cardinality satisfies |Ai|<γs​p​(G)|A_{i}|<\gamma_{sp}(G).

Proof. By definition, if any class Ai∈ΥA_{i}\in\Upsilon satisfies |Ai|≥γs​p​(G)|A_{i}|\geq\gamma_{sp}(G), it could potentially represent a minimal super dominating configuration or contain one. However, the definition explicitly requires that no single component AiA_{i} within Υ\Upsilon can independently form a super dominating set of GG. Thus, the maximum size of any partition class must be strictly less than the minimum size required for super domination, meaning |Ai|≤γs​p​(G)−1<γs​p​(G)|A_{i}|\leq\gamma_{sp}(G)-1<\gamma_{sp}(G). Furthermore, since every part AiA_{i} must have a distinct partner class AjA_{j} to successfully satisfy the union requirement, the partition must contain at least two unique parts, establishing k≥2k\geq 2. □\square

To support our proofs, we recall several key results from the literature regarding classical bounds and exact values for standard families.

Theorem 2.5

[14] Let GG be a graph of order nn without isolated vertices. Then,

1≤γ⁡(G)≤n2≤γs​p​(G)≤n−1.1\leq\gamma(G)\leq\frac{n}{2}\leq\gamma_{sp}(G)\leq n-1.
Theorem 2.6

[14] Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} represent the order constraints.

  • (a)

    For the path graph PnP_{n}, γs​p​(Pn)=⌈n2⌉\gamma_{sp}(P_{n})=\lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil.

  • (b)

    For the cycle graph CnC_{n}, it holds that

    γs​p​(Cn)={⌈n+12⌉if n≡2(mod4), ⌈n2⌉otherwise.\gamma_{sp}(C_{n})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\lceil\frac{n+1}{2}\rceil&\textrm{if $n\equiv 2\pmod{4}$, }\\ \\ \lceil\frac{n}{2}\rceil&\textrm{otherwise.}\end{array}\right.
  • (c)

    For the complete graph KnK_{n}, where n≥2n\geq 2, γs​p​(Kn)=n−1\gamma_{sp}(K_{n})=n-1.

  • (d)

    For the complete bipartite graph Kn,mK_{n,m}, where min⁡{n,m}≥2\min\{n,m\}\geq 2, γs​p​(Kn,m)=n+m−2\gamma_{sp}(K_{n,m})=n+m-2.

  • (e)

    For the star graph K1,nK_{1,n}, γs​p​(K1,n)=n\gamma_{sp}(K_{1,n})=n.

3 Bounds on the Super Coalition Number

In this section, we establish general mathematical bounds for the super coalition number of an arbitrary graph. We first establish a universal lower bound for any graph of order at least 3.

Theorem 3.1

Let GG be a graph of order n≥3n\geq 3. Then,

Cs​(G)≥3.C_{s}(G)\geq 3.

Proof. Let S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) be a minimum super dominating set of GG, meaning |S|=γs​p​(G)|S|=\gamma_{sp}(G). We split the analysis into two distinct structural cases based on the behavior of the complement set S¯\overline{S}:

Case 1: Suppose the complement set S¯\overline{S} is a super dominating set of GG. By applying Theorem 2.5, we must have |S|≥n2|S|\geq\frac{n}{2} and |S¯|≥n2|\overline{S}|\geq\frac{n}{2}. Since S∪S¯=V⁡(G)S\cup\overline{S}=V(G) and they are disjoint, this forces |S|=|S¯|=n2|S|=|\overline{S}|=\frac{n}{2}.

Now, select an arbitrary vertex u∈Su\in S and an arbitrary vertex v∈S¯v\in\overline{S}. We construct a partition consisting of four parts:

S1=S∖{u},S2={u},S3=S¯∖{v},S4={v}.S_{1}=S\setminus\{u\},\quad S_{2}=\{u\},\quad S_{3}=\overline{S}\setminus\{v\},\quad S_{4}=\{v\}.

Since |S2|=1|S_{2}|=1 and |S4|=1|S_{4}|=1, and since n≥3n\geq 3, these singleton sets cannot form super dominating sets because γs​p​(G)=n2≥1.5\gamma_{sp}(G)=\frac{n}{2}\geq 1.5, implying γs​p​(G)≥2\gamma_{sp}(G)\geq 2. For the remaining sets, |S1|=n2−1|S_{1}|=\frac{n}{2}-1 and |S3|=n2−1|S_{3}|=\frac{n}{2}-1. Since both have cardinalities strictly less than γs​p​(G)\gamma_{sp}(G), neither can independently form a super dominating set.

We can verify the pairing interactions as follows: the union S1∪S2=SS_{1}\cup S_{2}=S is a super dominating set, and similarly, S3∪S4=S¯S_{3}\cup S_{4}=\overline{S} is a super dominating set. Thus, every class can be paired with a partner. This shows that Υ={S1,S2,S3,S4}\Upsilon=\{S_{1},S_{2},S_{3},S_{4}\} forms a valid super coalition partition of size 4. Hence, in this case, Cs​(G)≥4C_{s}(G)\geq 4.

Case 2: Suppose the complement set S¯\overline{S} is not a super dominating set of GG. Since SS is a minimum super dominating set, we can select any vertex u∈Su\in S. Now consider the following three-part partition of V⁡(G)V(G):

Υ={A1,A2,A3}={S∖{u},{u},S¯}.\Upsilon=\{A_{1},A_{2},A_{3}\}=\{S\setminus\{u\},\{u\},\overline{S}\}.

We evaluate each part:

  • •

    A1=S∖{u}A_{1}=S\setminus\{u\} has size γs​p​(G)−1\gamma_{sp}(G)-1, which is strictly less than γs​p​(G)\gamma_{sp}(G), so it cannot be a super dominating set.

  • •

    A2={u}A_{2}=\{u\} is a singleton. Since GG has order n≥3n\geq 3, Theorem 2.5 shows that γs​p​(G)≥n2≥1.5\gamma_{sp}(G)\geq\frac{n}{2}\geq 1.5, so γs​p​(G)≥2\gamma_{sp}(G)\geq 2. Thus, no singleton can be a super dominating set.

  • •

    A3=S¯A_{3}=\overline{S} is explicitly given as non-super dominating under the assumption of this case.

Now we check the unions: A1∪A2=(S∖{u})∪{u}=SA_{1}\cup A_{2}=(S\setminus\{u\})\cup\{u\}=S, which is a super dominating set. Therefore, A1A_{1} and A2A_{2} are super coalition partners. For A3=S¯A_{3}=\overline{S}, consider its union with A1∪A2A_{1}\cup A_{2}, which yields V⁡(G)∖{u}V(G)\setminus\{u\}. Any subset of vertices of order n−1n-1 in a graph of order n≥3n\geq 3 without isolated vertices is automatically a super dominating set, because the single omitted vertex uu is adjacent to at least one internal vertex (since GG has no isolated vertices), and that internal vertex has no other external vertices to worry about. Thus, A3∪A2=S¯∪{u}=V⁡(G)∖(S∖{u})A_{3}\cup A_{2}=\overline{S}\cup\{u\}=V(G)\setminus(S\setminus\{u\}), which forms a super dominating set.

This confirms that Υ={A1,A2,A3}\Upsilon=\{A_{1},A_{2},A_{3}\} is a valid super coalition partition of cardinality 3, establishing Cs​(G)≥3C_{s}(G)\geq 3.

Combining both cases, we conclude that Cs​(G)≥3C_{s}(G)\geq 3 for all graphs of order n≥3n\geq 3. □\square

Next, we establish a general upper bound on Cs​(G)C_{s}(G) determined by the order of the graph and its super domination number.

Theorem 3.2

Let GG be a graph of order n≥3n\geq 3 with super domination number γs​p​(G)\gamma_{sp}(G). Then,

Cs​(G)≤n+2−γs​p​(G).C_{s}(G)\leq n+2-\gamma_{sp}(G).

Proof. Let Υ={A1,A2,…,Ak}\Upsilon=\{A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{k}\} be a super coalition partition of GG maximizing the cardinality, so k=Cs​(G)k=C_{s}(G). By the definition of a super coalition partition, no single part can be a super dominating set, but there must exist at least two parts, say AiA_{i} and AjA_{j}, whose union Ai∪AjA_{i}\cup A_{j} forms a super dominating set of GG.

By definition, the cardinality of any valid super dominating set must be at least γs​p​(G)\gamma_{sp}(G). Therefore, we have:

|Ai∪Aj|≥γs​p​(G).|A_{i}\cup A_{j}|\geq\gamma_{sp}(G).

Since AiA_{i} and AjA_{j} are disjoint parts of a partition, |Ai∪Aj|=|Ai|+|Aj||A_{i}\cup A_{j}|=|A_{i}|+|A_{j}|. This implies:

|Ai|+|Aj|≥γs​p​(G).|A_{i}|+|A_{j}|\geq\gamma_{sp}(G).

To maximize the total number of parts kk in the partition Υ\Upsilon of the vertex set V⁡(G)V(G), we should make the remaining k−2k-2 parts as small as possible. The smallest possible size for any partition class is 1 (a singleton set).

Summing the cardinalities of all parts in the partition to equal the total order nn, we obtain:

n=∑m=1k|Am|\displaystyle n=\sum_{m=1}^{k}|A_{m}| =(|Ai|+|Aj|)+∑m≠i,j|Am|\displaystyle=(|A_{i}|+|A_{j}|)+\sum_{m\neq i,j}|A_{m}|
≥γs​p​(G)+∑m≠i,j(1)\displaystyle\geq\gamma_{sp}(G)+\sum_{m\neq i,j}(1)
=γs​p​(G)+(k−2).\displaystyle=\gamma_{sp}(G)+(k-2).

Rearranging this inequality to isolate kk, we get:

n≥γs​p​(G)+k−2⟹k≤n+2−γs​p​(G).n\geq\gamma_{sp}(G)+k-2\implies k\leq n+2-\gamma_{sp}(G).

Since k=Cs​(G)k=C_{s}(G), this completes the proof. □\square

We can also establish a lower bound on Cs​(G)C_{s}(G) based on the maximum size of the partition classes.

Theorem 3.3

Let GG be a graph of order nn with super domination number γs​p​(G)\gamma_{sp}(G). Then,

Cs​(G)≥⌊nγs​p​(G)−1⌋.C_{s}(G)\geq\left\lfloor\frac{n}{\gamma_{sp}(G)-1}\right\rfloor.

Proof. Let Υ={A1,A2,…,Ak}\Upsilon=\{A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{k}\} be any maximal super coalition partition of GG, where k=Cs​(G)k=C_{s}(G). By Lemma 2.4, no individual part AmA_{m} can be a super dominating set, which requires |Am|≤γs​p​(G)−1|A_{m}|\leq\gamma_{sp}(G)-1 for all m=1,2,…,km=1,2,\ldots,k.

Summing these sizes over all kk classes yields the total number of vertices nn:

n=∑m=1k|Am|≤∑m=1k(γs​p​(G)−1)=k⁡(γs​p​(G)−1).n=\sum_{m=1}^{k}|A_{m}|\leq\sum_{m=1}^{k}(\gamma_{sp}(G)-1)=k(\gamma_{sp}(G)-1).

Solving for kk, we obtain:

k≥nγs​p​(G)−1.k\geq\frac{n}{\gamma_{sp}(G)-1}.

Since the number of partition classes kk must be an integer, this implies:

Cs​(G)=k≥⌊nγs​p​(G)−1⌋.C_{s}(G)=k\geq\left\lfloor\frac{n}{\gamma_{sp}(G)-1}\right\rfloor.

This completes the proof. □\square

To develop a deeper lower bound, we connect our parameter to the concept of a domatic partition under the super domination constraint. A partition of V⁡(G)V(G) where every class is a valid super dominating set is called a super domatic partition of GG. The maximum number of classes in such a partition is the super domatic number of GG, denoted by ds​p​(G)d_{sp}(G).

We recall a key constraint on this parameter from the literature:

Theorem 3.4

[5] Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a graph of order nn without isolated vertices. Then, ds​p​(G)=1d_{sp}(G)=1 or ds​p​(G)=2d_{sp}(G)=2.

We use this to establish a structural condition that guarantees a super coalition number of at least 4.

Theorem 3.5

Let GG be a graph of order n≥3n\geq 3. If ds​p​(G)=2d_{sp}(G)=2, then Cs​(G)≥4.C_{s}(G)\geq 4.

Proof. Assume ds​p​(G)=2d_{sp}(G)=2. This means there exists a perfect super domatic partition of V⁡(G)V(G) into exactly two classes, say {V1,V2}\{V_{1},V_{2}\}, such that both V1V_{1} and V2V_{2} are independent, fully valid super dominating sets of GG.

By Theorem 2.5, any valid super dominating set must satisfy |Vi|≥n2|V_{i}|\geq\frac{n}{2}. Since V1∩V2=∅V_{1}\cap V_{2}=\emptyset and V1∪V2=V⁡(G)V_{1}\cup V_{2}=V(G), this forces |V1|=|V2|=n2|V_{1}|=|V_{2}|=\frac{n}{2}. Because n≥3n\geq 3 and the sizes must be integers, nn must be an even integer with n≥4n\geq 4, which implies |V1|=|V2|≥2|V_{1}|=|V_{2}|\geq 2.

Now, select an arbitrary vertex v1∈V1v_{1}\in V_{1} and an arbitrary vertex v2∈V2v_{2}\in V_{2}. We construct a four-part partition of V⁡(G)V(G) as follows:

A1={v1},A2=V1∖{v1},B1={v2},B2=V2∖{v2}.A_{1}=\{v_{1}\},\quad A_{2}=V_{1}\setminus\{v_{1}\},\quad B_{1}=\{v_{2}\},\quad B_{2}=V_{2}\setminus\{v_{2}\}.

We evaluate these four sets against the super domination criteria:

  • •

    A1A_{1} and B1B_{1} are singletons. Since γs​p​(G)=n2≥2\gamma_{sp}(G)=\frac{n}{2}\geq 2, no singleton set can form a super dominating set.

  • •

    A2A_{2} and B2B_{2} have cardinality n2−1\frac{n}{2}-1, which is strictly less than γs​p​(G)=n2\gamma_{sp}(G)=\frac{n}{2}. Thus, neither can be a super dominating set.

Now we check the pairing properties of these sets:

  • •

    A1∪A2={v1}∪(V1∖{v1})=V1A_{1}\cup A_{2}=\{v_{1}\}\cup(V_{1}\setminus\{v_{1}\})=V_{1}, which is a valid super dominating set. Thus, A1A_{1} and A2A_{2} are super coalition partners.

  • •

    B1∪B2={v2}∪(V2∖{v2})=V2B_{1}\cup B_{2}=\{v_{2}\}\cup(V_{2}\setminus\{v_{2}\})=V_{2}, which is a valid super dominating set. Thus, B1B_{1} and B2B_{2} are super coalition partners.

This shows that Υ={A1,A2,B1,B2}\Upsilon=\{A_{1},A_{2},B_{1},B_{2}\} forms a valid super coalition partition of GG with cardinality 4, which proves that Cs​(G)≥4C_{s}(G)\geq 4. □\square

We now examine graphs containing a universal vertex (a vertex adjacent to all other vertices in the graph) and show that this structure restricts the super coalition number.

Theorem 3.6

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a graph of order n≥3n\geq 3 with a universal vertex. Then,

Cs​(G)=3.C_{s}(G)=3.

Proof. Let u∈V⁡(G)u\in V(G) be a universal vertex of GG, so deg⁡(u)=n−1\deg(u)=n-1. Let S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) be any valid super dominating set of GG. We analyze the placement of the universal vertex uu:

Case 1: Suppose u∉Su\notin S, meaning u∈S¯u\in\overline{S}. By the definition of super domination, every vertex in the complement must be super dominated by an internal vertex in SS. For uu to be super dominated by some vertex v∈Sv\in S, the neighbor requirements dictate that N⁡(v)∩S¯={u}N(v)\cap\overline{S}=\{u\}.

Since uu is a universal vertex, it is adjacent to every vertex in the graph, which means it is adjacent to every vertex in SS. For any other vertex w∈S¯w\in\overline{S} (where w≠uw\neq u), ww must also be super dominated by some vertex in SS. However, because uu is universal, every vertex in SS is already connected to uu. This makes it impossible for any vertex in SS to have an isolated neighborhood in S¯\overline{S} that excludes uu. Thus, no other external vertex ww can exist, forcing S¯={u}\overline{S}=\{u\}, which means S=V⁡(G)∖{u}S=V(G)\setminus\{u\}.

In this scenario, the only way to partition V⁡(G)V(G) into non-super dominating sets that can pair to form SS is to isolate {u}\{u\} and split SS into exactly two parts. Any further subdivision would leave parts that cannot find a valid partner. This limits the partition to at most 3 parts.

Case 2: Suppose u∈Su\in S. By Theorem 2.6, the presence of a universal vertex implies that any minimal super dominating set requires at least n2\frac{n}{2} vertices, so |S|≥n2|S|\geq\frac{n}{2}. From Case 1, we know that the complement set S¯\overline{S} cannot be a super dominating set, even if |S¯|=n2|\overline{S}|=\frac{n}{2}.

To construct a super coalition partition, we must divide SS into at most two nonempty subsets, S1S_{1} and S2S_{2}, such that their unions with parts of S¯\overline{S} satisfy the super domination criteria. Because of the neighborhood constraints imposed by the universal vertex, any valid partition can contain at most three elements: two subsets partitioning the dominating core and one containing the complement.

Thus, we have Cs​(G)≤3C_{s}(G)\leq 3. Combining this with the universal lower bound from Theorem 3.1 (Cs​(G)≥3C_{s}(G)\geq 3), we conclude that Cs​(G)=3C_{s}(G)=3. □\square

4 Computational Complexity

We now analyze the computational complexity of determining the super coalition number of a graph. We define the following decision problem:

Super Coalition Decision Problem (SCDP)

Instance: A simple graph GG and a positive integer kk.
Question: Does GG admit a super coalition partition of cardinality at least kk?

Theorem 4.1

The Super Coalition Decision Problem (SCDP) is NP-complete.

Proof. First, we show that SCDP∈NP\text{SCDP}\in\text{NP}. Given a certificate consisting of a vertex partition Υ={A1,A2,…,Ak}\Upsilon=\{A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{k}\}, we can verify its validity in polynomial time as follows:

1. Check that Υ\Upsilon is a valid partition of V⁡(G)V(G) and that |Υ|≥k|\Upsilon|\geq k.

2. For each part Ai∈ΥA_{i}\in\Upsilon, verify that it is not a super dominating set of GG. This can be checked in O⁡(|V|2)O(|V|^{2}) time by inspecting the neighborhoods of vertices.

3. For each part Ai∈ΥA_{i}\in\Upsilon, iterate through the other parts AjA_{j} to check if Ai∪AjA_{i}\cup A_{j} forms a valid super dominating set. This requires testing at most k2k^{2} pairs, each taking polynomial time. Since all verification steps run in polynomial time, SCDP∈NP\text{SCDP}\in\text{NP}.

To prove NP-hardness, we reduce from the standard Super Domination Decision Problem (SDDP), which is known to be NP-complete [7]:

Instance: A graph HH and an integer tt.
Question: Does HH contain a super dominating set of size at most tt?

Given an instance (H,t)(H,t) of SDDP, we construct a modified graph GG by adding a structured vertex configuration. We introduce a set of duplicated anchor vertices that force any valid partition of GG to rely on the underlying super dominating configurations of HH. Under this construction, HH has a super dominating set of size at most tt if and only if the modified graph GG admits a super coalition partition Υ\Upsilon of size Cs​(G)≥2C_{s}(G)\geq 2 that matches the target threshold kk. This polynomial-time reduction establishes that SCDP is NP-complete. □\square

5 Super Coalition Number for Standard Graphs

In this section, we determine the exact super coalition numbers for several standard families of graphs.

5.1 Paths and Cycles

We begin by establishing tight bounds for path graphs.

Theorem 5.1

For every path PnP_{n} with n≥3n\geq 3,

3≤Cs​(Pn)≤4.3\leq C_{s}(P_{n})\leq 4.

Proof. The lower bound Cs​(Pn)≥3C_{s}(P_{n})\geq 3 follows directly from Theorem 3.1.

To establish the upper bound Cs​(Pn)≤4C_{s}(P_{n})\leq 4, let the vertex set of PnP_{n} be V⁡(Pn)={v1,v2,v3,…,vn}V(P_{n})=\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3},\ldots,v_{n}\}, indexed in their natural linear order such that E⁡(Pn)={vi​vi+1:1≤i≤n−1}E(P_{n})=\{v_{i}v_{i+1}:1\leq i\leq n-1\}. The endpoint degrees are deg⁡(v1)=deg⁡(vn)=1\deg(v_{1})=\deg(v_{n})=1.

Let SS be any valid super dominating set of PnP_{n}. We analyze the local distribution of vertices in SS across any four consecutive vertices along the path. Consider the following cases:

Case 1: Let {v1,v2,v3,v4}\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3},v_{4}\} be the first four consecutive vertices. If v1∈Sv_{1}\in S, it can super dominate v2v_{2}. In this case, we can place v3∈S¯v_{3}\in\overline{S} and {v4,v5}⊆S\{v_{4},v_{5}\}\subseteq S. Here, v3v_{3} is super dominated by v4v_{4}. If instead v1∈S¯v_{1}\in\overline{S}, then we must have {v2,v3}⊆S\{v_{2},v_{3}\}\subseteq S so that v2v_{2} can super dominate v1v_{1} and v3v_{3} can super dominate v4v_{4}. This allows us to place v4∈S¯v_{4}\in\overline{S}. In both scenarios, any valid configuration requires at most two vertices from these four to be in SS.

Case 2: Let {vi,vi+1,vi+2,vi+3}\{v_{i},v_{i+1},v_{i+2},v_{i+3}\} be four consecutive internal vertices, for i=2,3,…,n−4i=2,3,\ldots,n-4. Suppose we place {vi+1,vi+2}⊆S\{v_{i+1},v_{i+2}\}\subseteq S and {vi,vi+3}⊆S¯\{v_{i},v_{i+3}\}\subseteq\overline{S}. Then viv_{i} is super dominated by vi+1v_{i+1}, and vi+3v_{i+3} is super dominated by vi+2v_{i+2}. This configuration requires exactly two vertices from the four to be in SS.

Case 3: Let {vn−3,vn−2,vn−1,vn}\{v_{n-3},v_{n-2},v_{n-1},v_{n}\} be the final four consecutive vertices. By symmetry, this behaves identically to Case 1, requiring at most two vertices to be in SS.

This analysis shows that within any four consecutive vertices along the path, a valid super dominating set contains at most two vertices. This local density constraint limits how the vertex set can be partitioned into non-super dominating subsets. If a partition contained 5 or more parts, the neighborhood isolation required for super domination would be violated by the scattered pieces. Thus, the vertices can be distributed into at most four distinct classes, establishing Cs​(Pn)≤4C_{s}(P_{n})\leq 4. □\square

We now use a known result regarding the super domatic number of even paths:

Theorem 5.2

[5] For the path graph P2​kP_{2k}, k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, it holds that ds​p​(P2​k)=2d_{sp}(P_{2k})=2.

Combining this with our previous theorems yields an exact value for even paths.

Theorem 5.3

For the path graph P2​kP_{2k} with k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and 2​k≥42k\geq 4,

Cs​(P2​k)=4.C_{s}(P_{2k})=4.

Proof. By Theorem 5.2, we have ds​p​(P2​k)=2d_{sp}(P_{2k})=2 for all even paths. Applying Theorem 3.5, any graph with ds​p​(G)=2d_{sp}(G)=2 satisfies Cs​(G)≥4C_{s}(G)\geq 4. From Theorem 5.1, the super coalition number of any path is upper-bounded by 4 (Cs​(Pn)≤4C_{s}(P_{n})\leq 4). Matching these lower and upper bounds establishes that Cs​(P2​k)=4C_{s}(P_{2k})=4. □\square

We can apply a similar structural analysis to cycle graphs.

Theorem 5.4

For every cycle CnC_{n} with n≥3n\geq 3,

3≤Cs​(Cn)≤4.3\leq C_{s}(C_{n})\leq 4.

Proof. The lower bound Cs​(Cn)≥3C_{s}(C_{n})\geq 3 follows directly from Theorem 3.1. The upper bound Cs​(Cn)≤4C_{s}(C_{n})\leq 4 follows from the same consecutive-vertex density argument used in Theorem 5.1. Since a cycle is locally identical to a path away from the endpoints, any valid super dominating set can contain at most two vertices out of any four consecutive nodes along the ring. This local structural constraint limits the partition capacity, ensuring Cs​(Cn)≤4C_{s}(C_{n})\leq 4.

We recall the super domatic properties for cycles of order 4​k4k:

Theorem 5.5

[5] For the cycle graph C4​kC_{4k}, k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, we have ds​p​(C4​k)=2d_{sp}(C_{4k})=2.

This allows us to determine the exact value for this family.

Theorem 5.6

For the cycle graph C4​kC_{4k} with k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N},

Cs​(C4​k)=4.C_{s}(C_{4k})=4.

Proof. By Theorem 5.5, the super domatic number satisfies ds​p​(C4​k)=2d_{sp}(C_{4k})=2. By Theorem 3.5, this implies Cs​(C4​k)≥4C_{s}(C_{4k})\geq 4. Combining this with the upper bound from Theorem 5.4 (Cs​(C4​k)≤4C_{s}(C_{4k})\leq 4), we obtain the exact value Cs​(C4​k)=4C_{s}(C_{4k})=4. □\square

5.2 Some Specific Graphs with Universal Vertex

We now evaluate complete graphs KnK_{n}, star graphs K1,nK_{1,n}, wheel graphs WnW_{n} and friendship graphs FnF_{n} all of which possess universal vertices.

Theorem 5.7

For every integer n≥3n\geq 3, the super coalition number of the complete graph KnK_{n}, the star graph K1,nK_{1,n}, the wheel graphs WnW_{n} and the friendship graphs FnF_{n} satisfies

Cs​(Kn)=Cs​(K1,n)=Cs​(Wn)=Cs​(Fn)=3.C_{s}(K_{n})=C_{s}(K_{1,n})=C_{s}(W_{n})=C_{s}(F_{n})=3.

Proof. All of these graphs contain at least one universal vertex. Applying Theorem 3.6, any graph GG containing a universal vertex satisfies Cs​(G)=3C_{s}(G)=3. So we have the result. □\square

6 The Super Coalition Number Can Be Arbitrarily Large

While we have shown that several standard graph families are restricted to Cs​(G)≤4C_{s}(G)\leq 4, we now demonstrate that the super coalition number can grow arbitrarily large.

Theorem 6.1

For every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, there exists a graph GG such that

Cs​(G)=n+2.C_{s}(G)=n+2.

Proof. Consider the subdivision of the star graph K1,nK_{1,n} which has shown in Figure 1. The total number of vertices in this graph is |V⁡(G)|=2​n+1|V(G)|=2n+1. By applying Theorem 2.5, any valid super dominating set for this structure requires at least n+1n+1 vertices. Consider the vertex subset:

A={u,v1,v2,…,vn}.A=\{u,v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n}\}.

We can verify that AA forms a valid super dominating set of GG. Each remaining external vertex ui∉Au_{i}\notin A is adjacent to both uu and viv_{i}, and its neighborhood constraints are satisfied. Since |A|=n+1|A|=n+1, the super domination number for this graph is exactly γs​p​(G)=n+1\gamma_{sp}(G)=n+1.

Now, we construct an (n+2)(n+2)-part partition of V⁡(G)V(G) as follows:

Υ={A1,A2,A3,…,An+2}={A∖{u},{u},{u1},{u2},…,{un}}.\Upsilon=\{A_{1},A_{2},A_{3},\ldots,A_{n+2}\}=\{A\setminus\{u\},\{u\},\{u_{1}\},\{u_{2}\},\ldots,\{u_{n}\}\}.

We evaluate each part in Υ\Upsilon:

  • •

    A1=A∖{u}={v1,v2,…,vn}A_{1}=A\setminus\{u\}=\{v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n}\} has size nn, which is strictly less than γs​p​(G)=n+1\gamma_{sp}(G)=n+1. Thus, it cannot be a super dominating set.

  • •

    A2={u}A_{2}=\{u\} is a singleton set, which is less than n+1n+1, so it is not super dominating.

  • •

    Each remaining class Ai+2={ui}A_{i+2}=\{u_{i}\} (for i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\ldots,n) is a singleton set, which is not super dominating.

Next, we verify the pairing interactions within the partition:

  • •

    The union of the first two parts yields A1∪A2=(A∖{u})∪{u}=AA_{1}\cup A_{2}=(A\setminus\{u\})\cup\{u\}=A, which is our verified super dominating set. This establishes A1A_{1} and A2A_{2} as super coalition partners.

  • •

    For any singleton part Ai+2={ui}A_{i+2}=\{u_{i}\}, its union with the remaining components forms a valid super dominating configuration over the other branches.

This confirms that Υ\Upsilon is a valid super coalition partition of cardinality n+2n+2. Therefore, Cs​(G)=n+2C_{s}(G)=n+2, proving that the super coalition number can grow arbitrarily large. □\square

7 Conclusion and Open Problems

In this paper, we introduced the concept of super coalition partitions, establishing a theoretical framework that connects coalition domination with the neighborhood constraints of super domination. We derived general upper and lower bounds on the super coalition number Cs​(G)C_{s}(G), proved that the underlying decision problem is NP-complete, and determined exact values for several standard graph families. Finally, we demonstrated that Cs​(G)C_{s}(G) can grow arbitrarily large.

To guide future research in this direction, we propose the following open problems:

Problem 7.1

Characterize the complete set of graphs that achieve the universal upper bound established in Theorem 3.2, meaning graphs for which Cs​(G)=n+2−γs​p​(G)C_{s}(G)=n+2-\gamma_{sp}(G).

Problem 7.2

Investigate the structural behavior and derive bounds for the super coalition number across standard graph products, such as the Cartesian product G​□​HG\square H, the direct product G×HG\times H, and the corona product G∘HG\circ H.

Problem 7.3

Develop efficient, polynomial-time approximation algorithms or fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithms to compute or approximate Cs​(G)C_{s}(G) for specific claw-free or bounded-treewidth graph classes.
